utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to use the time for at least one item on our procedural agenda. It deals with the remaining issue from the testimony of Milenko Jevtevic. During the testimony of Milenko Jevtevic on the 23rd of February of this year, P7137 was marked for identification, pending a revised English translation. On that same day, the Prosecution informed the Chamber via an e-mail that a revised translation had been uploaded into e-court under document ID 0107-7905-A-ET. If there are no objections and the Defence has an opportunity to revisit the matter within the next 48 hours, but the Chamber instructs the Registry to replace the existing English translation of P7137 with a new translation and admits P7137 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Franjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apologies for continuing with administrative matters when you entered the courtroom. Mr. Franjic, Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination, but I'd first like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to start with 65 ter number 1D5494 in e-court. While we wait for that, I can advise that this is a transcript of the testimony of a Prosecution expert witness at this trial, Timothy Curtis who was the chief operations officer for laboratory services for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives in the US, and a member of AFTE. If we can have page 19 in e-court, that should correlate with transcript page 14833, and we'll be starting at line 15, and I'll read for you, sir, so you can get the translation. "Q. Mr. Curtis, here, we see your name and signature and the name of three other persons and their signatures. Can you tell us the role that those three other persons played in the investigation and preparation of this report. "A. Yes, three of us were fire-arm examiners, myself, Mr. Danridge and Mr. Ols. And the three of us did the actual physical comparisons of the cartridge cases using the comparison microscopes to identify or eliminate cartridge cases being fired in the same fire-arms. Mr. Wilson, who is on the lower right, he was our section supervisor at the time, and his role was basically to review our paperwork and make sure it was proper, following all of our procedures, and afterwards, after we'd --"

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "... signed off on everything and he saw it was correct, he would then sign. "Q. And as an example in respect of the two matches we have identified for request number 5, do you know who it was that the verified your own findings that there had been a match? "A. Yes, Mr. Walter Danridge verified my positive identification on those two identifications. "Q. And how do you recall that? "A. After I verified it, I asked Mr. Danridge to look into the microscope. He came to the same conclusion as I did. I took a photograph, marked the front of it as you had seen, but on the back side, Mr. Danridge initialled and dated the photograph to verify that he agreed with my findings." And if we scroll down to the bottom of this page, at line 22, starting with the text, it says: "Q. The methods of analysis employed by the ATF, both the IBIS preliminary analysis phase and the microscopic analysis phase, were they consistent with -- or are they consistent with prevailing industry standards?" If we could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This was a question put to that witness at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said starting with the text and you followed immediately an answer and then you say it is follows down to the page and then it should be clear that it was a new question that was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe I mentioned there was a question. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please reread the transcript and tell me later where you introduced this portion, last portion you read, by saying that it was a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe line 22 of the page where the quotation I start with said it was a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the transcriber did for you, Mr. Ivetic, and that's very kind of her. Please proceed. And if I'm wrong, then, of course, I'll verify it, if my recollection doesn't serve me well, Mr. Ivetic, I'm the first one to admit that, and I may even listen to the audio whether it's indeed the transcriber or whether I just missed it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "A. Yes. The procedures we used back in 2000 are basically the same procedures that are following today as far as comparisons of evidence on comparison microscope and working with the IBIS system." Do you agree with Mr. Curtis that this method of analysis of marking on a photograph and having a second examiner initial the back of the photograph after verifying the conclusions is the method of analysis consistent with the prevailing industry standard for this type of review.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you stated has to do with performing analyses in the laboratory. As far as our laboratory is concerned, in our lab for mechanoscopic analysis, we use a different procedure. We perform comparative analysis of the disputed cartridges. We also analyse and compare the disputed cartridges as opposed to undisputed ones. We also mutually compare the disputed rounds against each other, as well as disputed rounds against undisputed rounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, if I may stop you there. I think you missed the gist of the question. The question was that marking a photograph, a photograph made of -- through the comparison microscope and have a second examiner look at it and then to initial the back of that photograph, so that it is, rather, two persons closely working together and recording their findings, whether that is the standard. Because there seems to be no dispute that you did more or less the same. That is, to compare the marks on disputed cartridges and known cartridges or two disputed cartridges, to see whether they were fired from the same weapon. It's two persons, identifying and recording, whether that's the standard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not familiar with that, but as in my previous testimony where I cited my first expert report, I can say again that in addition to me performing the work, the same rounds and cartridges were examined by a ballistics and mechanoscopic expert, Alija Kotarevic. We provided a joint report, and we agreed that the seven cartridges originate from bullets fired from one and the same weapon. As for the other disputed cartridges and rounds, our opinion is also provided in our expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could take a look at 1D5492 with you. While we wait for it, I can introduce it as the Code of Ethnics for the AFTE as published on their official web site. First of all, sir, can you tell me if you are familiar with the AFTE Code of Ethnics?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to page 2, and if we could ... look at -- I apologise. It's the next page, page 3. And item number H at the top, the third bullet number from the top where it says: "Any and all photographic displays shall be made according to accepted [sic] practices, and shall not be ... altered or distorted with a view to mislead the court or jury." Sir, do you feel that your reports which failed to provide photographic depictions of the comparison and matching analysis adhere to this provision of the AFTE Code of Ethnics?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sort of puzzled which that question, Mr. Ivetic. Obviously we didn't adhere with the situation where this witness didn't make photographs, and this rule doesn't say all investigations must be photographed but they say, where photographs have been, taken, then there must be done according to acceptable standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that is why in my question I did not state affirmatively that he had not complied. I'm asking the witness whether he believes that that condition does apply, given the testimony of Mr. Curtis that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I'll understand as we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you answer the question as it was put to you by Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This cannot be directly linked to the expert report produced by myself and my colleague. The microscopic photographs were not taken using a comparative microscope to photograph the markings. The photographs that were taken were not altered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to look at item number IV on this page, section A or subpart A: "No services shall be rendered on a contingency fee basis." In relation to the cash prizes that you have received and recorded in your CV, especially the one from the federal police directorate "for outstanding work results," have you ever sought an advisory opinion from AFTE to determine if such cash awards for your work do not run afoul of this provision?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to your first report, which will be P7434 marked for identification, and I would ask that we look at page 106 in the English and page 65 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, could I receive a copy of my report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means if my colleagues have it. Just as with yesterday, I don't have any problem with the witness getting it directly. And so in the B/C/S, it's page 65 in e-court but I believe it will be page 64 of the hard copy on the bottom, the numbering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that English or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was for B/C/S for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know the page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that before, I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. It should be in the middle of the page in English and the third bullet point from the bottom in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here you identify artefact 34B as an M49 round having come from a 7.9 by 57 millimetre M48 army rifle. First of all, sir, am I correct that this round is commonly referred to in the industry as an 8-millimetre Mauser round?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can now call up 1D5459, and page 3 in e-court of the same. Sir, looking at the picture on the top of the page of a bolt-action rifle with a bayonet, is this, in fact, the M48 army rifle that you referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, for purposes of your analysis, did you take into account and perform analysis of any other weapons that are capable of firing the 8-millimetre Mauser round, 7.9 by 57 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. How many other weapons did you consider?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: M48, M48A, and I can't recall right now what other rifles, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's see if can I assist you. Let's look at 1D5460.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me. We should probably since we looked at a photograph, I would ask that we reserve a number for this last document 1D5459, so that I can just get the photograph separated from the rest of the documentation and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please reserve a number for that specific part of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number reserved for document 1D5459 will be D1086, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, again, if we could have 1D5460.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this is again from the Igman Unis Company and it shows two types of bullets, 7.9 by 57. Would you agree with me -- actually, let's go to page 2. That will be easier. Whoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe we're using the wrong version of the document. There should be two in e-court one that has a corrected page 2. Because I noted that this version has two identical pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Madam Registrar couldn't know which has the correct page 2, so, therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I know. I know. I apologise. It's the same? Okay. Let's ... let me do it this way, then, sir. Go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, looking at the bullet that's on the left, the cartridge on the round that's on the left that's labelled as a 7.957 M49 Ball, would that be similar to the M49 round that we've been talking about in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the round is M49 and the bullet is as we can see. So the round originated from this bullet which was 7.9 by 57-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, to try to see what other weapons you might have excluded, according to the manufacturer's information, the M53 light machine-gun also can fire this round, is that in accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: M53 is a full machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... fire this same round?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can fire it, but the common general characteristics are not the same, compared to rounds fired from an army rifle M48. In my expert report, on page 65, I state - or we state - that the disputed deformed and damaged round, M49 of 7.9 by 57-millimetre calibre marked as 34B may originate from a bullet fired from an army rifle M48. So, it may be. I am not asserting that it was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does that mean that your report excludes the possibility that an M53 fired this questioned round?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what about an M84? Does that also fire the same round, also a full machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It doesn't. It can't, because M84 machine-gun is of 7.62-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, getting back to the M48 Mauser-style rifle, would be surprised to learn that the 8-millimetre Mauser round is considered to be a round that's also used in sporting and hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it has to have a lead tip. It has to be a soft point bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And ... would you agree that at least since 1980 the 8-millimetre Mauser round that -- pardon me. At least since 1980 hunting rifles have been chambered to fire the 8-millimetre Mauser round?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The calibre of hunting rifles is 8 by 57 millimetres, and this is 7.9. According to what I know, it is dangerous to test fire these bullets from hunting rifles whose calibre is 8 by 5.7 millimetres. They can be fired, but there is a danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In 1992, could the M48 be owned by civilians?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, so I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we could look at P2894 in e-court, and while we wait for it, it should be a report of the Prijedor SJB dated 2 August 1992 and it reports on weapons confiscated from persons up until 31 July 1992, and we see that seven M48 rifles were in the possession of the police confiscated from someone. Would you agree with me that without further testing, we cannot exclude the possibility that your unknown M49 rounds originated from one of these seven M48 rifles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, my question is whether this is in the realm of the -- of the expertise of this witness; and the second question is whether it's not -- it's -- doesn't it go without saying that if a bullet can be fired by a certain weapon and if that weapon may have been - and the witness refrained from any comment on that - in the hands of civilians, that civilians then could have fired those bullets? Just on the very abstract level apart from all other matters to be considered, who would have fired those weapons. I never noticed also on the report that the witness considered it to be within his expertise to say anything about the quality or the qualification or the identity of persons firing those weapons and that he limited himself - perhaps rightly so - to the analysis of the weapons and the cartridges and the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may try to understand, my question is based on the science that he employs and what other scientists of his nature would employ that in fact to show it's not just an army rifle, that other entities have that same rifle. So there's no misunderstanding when looking at the report because he calls it an army rifle. It is a rifle being used by the army or that agree that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered that by saying I have no -- I have no answer to your question whether it would have been in the hands of civilians, which already explains that what he calls an army rifle may not exclusively be in the hands of persons employed by the army that and's -- I think that's obvious, but I'm also looking at the Prosecution. If there's no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, there's no dispute about that, Your Honours, and you know, page 11, line 18 and 19, the witness has clearly indicated that he isn't in a position to say yes or no whether an M48 was owned by civilians, to follow up further doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if this witness certainly does not exclude that, the Chamber of course will consider, if we're talking about weapons, who may have fired those weapons. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we can move on to ... number 32671 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document from the Prijedor police dated June 1992, I believe 9 June, giving -- giving information on weapons that they have available, and we see here two different variants of the M70 chambered at 7.62 round in total I think is approximately 966 such weapons. Could both variants of the M70 listed here fire the 7.62 by 39-millimetre cartridge M67 round which was analysed by you in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: M70/31 and M70/32, I'm not familiar with these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, what's in dispute here are 12 rounds whose calibre was 7.62 by 39 millimetres. They could have been fired from this type of weapon which is mentioned in here. So M70, as I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to assist those that may not be familiar with the abbreviations as you and I. The PAP 7.62 millimetre of which there are 450 items in the inventory, is this in fact the M59/66 semi-automatic that we talked about in the previous days?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the abbreviation PAP stands for semi-automatic weapon or rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I wish to return to your first report, P7434 MFI, before we do, for the 7.62 by 39-millimetre round, would you also agree with me that we have no way of knowing whose rifle or rifles fired the rounds that you analysed? We just know they came from a specific type of rifle that was very widespread in its circulation.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your report -- oops, P7434, MFI, it will be page 18 in the B/C/S in e-court, which means it will be the page marked 17 on the bottom for you, sir, in the hard copy; and it will be page 26 in English. And it will be in relation -- it will be at the top in B/C/S and the second paragraph in English. You identify a certain pistol ammunition including this disputed and unfired round next to the body TOM-04-PRD 003. Now, in your report, you state that this is a 7.65 by 17-millimetre round produced by Igman Konjic in 1983. Now, with all due respect to you, sir, I believe you are wrong in your conclusion as it is written here. Would you take a moment to consider and tell me if you agree with me.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, it was a mistake. The producer was Prvi Partizan from Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Year of production, 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now apart from that misidentification of the manufacturer, let's focus now on the round. The 7.65 by 17-millimetre round is identified in relation to three bullets you analysed for TOM-04-PRD 260T. That's at page 48 in the B/C/S, 74 in the English. And in both instances, you identified the known round as possibly coming from a Zastava M70 pistol, and your findings are on page 106 in the English and page 66 in the B/C/S. And by my count, there's also one other disputed round of the same type, 7.65 by 17 millimetres and that is in your second report, P7435, MFI, in relation to TOM-04-PRD 383T and that's to be found in page 13 of both languages, photos 24 through 25 and, again, a Crvena Zastava M70 semi-automatic pistol is identified as a possible source. Now, with respect to all of these pistol rounds that you analysed, I believe five in total, were they also analysed with respect to known fired rounds from other pistols of the same calibre to exclude them as a possible source?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that that analysis is not recorded in your written report?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to 1D05474 in e-court. And if we look at the photograph of what is referred to by Wikipedia as the .32 ACP is, in fact, the round we've been talking about the 7.65 by 17-millimetre pistol round commonly referred to see at .32 automatic or .32 ACP. Is that the same bullet that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same bullet but the manufacturer is different. However, it's, in essence, one and the same bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 in e-court, we will see a listing of prominent fire-arms chambered in .32 ACP and we see 18 models on this page, starting with the Beretta M1935. And if we turn to the next page, I think we have another 26 fire-arms listed, the last of which is the Zastava M70. How many of these different models chambered to fire the same bullet were analysed and excluded as being a possible source for the rounds that you reviewed as part of your report?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you which ones I examined, but before I do that, I would like to say that we have established that the disputable bullet, 7.65 by 17, marked as 2, the deformed bullet and the casing, marked by numbers 3 and 4, 04-PRD 260D [as interpreted] could originate from the bullets fired from a semi-automatic pistol, M72, Crvena Zastava of 7.65-millimetre calibre. I'm not claiming that they were indeed fired from that pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I understand. That's why I said possibly can any of these other guns chambered to fire the same bullet possibly be the source of that bullet, according to your review?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be. When it comes to bullets, it's very difficult to establish the brand, the model, and the type of the fire-arm, and especially if the fire-arm is a pistol. It's very difficult to determine the brand, model, and type.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And so when you put in your report that it could have come from an M72 -- pardon me. Did you say M72 or M70?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought so but the transcript had M72. When you say that in your report that it could have come from an M70 to be entirely accurate it should have also said or several other fire-arms of the same chambered calibre?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the calibre would not have been the same. The most important thing is that they should have had common general characteristics and one of those characteristics is calibre. So that's what we have to say. The number of grooves, the number of lands, the breadth, the width of lands and grooves, all that has to be taken into account as common general characteristics. What we have found were common general characteristics which matched the bullets fired from an M70 Zastava pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, earlier you said that you had looked at some of these other types of fire-arms that fired that round. Could you tell us which ones you did analyse as part of your analysis and whether you excluded them as potentially being the source of the fired round that -- fired rounds that you examined?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of those that you reviewed, did you, in fact, exclude or leave the possibility that they could have been fired from those pistols that you reviewed but which you do not remember which ones they were?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I excluded those. To be more precise, we excluded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Crvena Zastava M70, if we could turn to 1D05475 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, I would ask to tender the last one we looked at, 1D5474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5474 receives number D1087, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection to that one, but since we're at the tendering phase, I wonder if, also, the previous document shown to the witness and that he commented on, it would also make sense to tender that, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 32671 receives number D1088, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the photograph of the fire-arm depicted here for those less familiar with them, sir, is this, in fact, the Yugoslav Zastava semi-automatic M70 pistol that we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, this source states for this pistol and I now quote at the bottom of the page in English: "The M70 pistol was produced by Yugoslavian (now Serbian) arms factory Crvena Zastava as a side-arm for police and certain military officers." Does that accord with your knowledge and research into this pistol?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would not volunteer an answer to this question because I don't think that it is within the scope of my expertise and my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was the M70 pistol the official side-arm of several MUP entities within the former Yugoslavia, most notably the Republic of Croatia, both before and during the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would not wish to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you happen to know if the M70 pistol was available for sale to private citizens prior to 1992 in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5475 receives number D1089, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 10.30, time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you give us an indication as to how much time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes after the break. Mr. Franjic, we'd like to see you back after the break, that is, after 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom, Mr. Ivetic, I was wrong when I said earlier today that it was the court reporter who said "question," because it was you yourself, so therefore, I think it was on page 4, line 20, my comment was wrong, and I should have thought about it before I made it. Apologies for that. We then -- I then move to -- if there is, no, there's no sufficient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your reports, you also talk about another pistol type of ammunition, the 7.62 by 25-millimetre round and in your conclusions you say that it is similar to a known bullet fired from a Crvena Zastava M57 pistol. In the first report, P7434 MFI, we see that at page 26 in the English, page 17 in the B/C/S, in relation to TOM-04-PRD 202T and photo number 68, and we also see it at page 31 in the B/C/S, 46 in the English, photos 110 to 112 in relation to TOM-04-PRD 420T and lastly also -- strike that. Also in regard to page 56 through 57 of the B/C/S, page 90 of the English, photos 194 through 195, in relation to TOM-04-PRD 158T and then in the second report, P7435 MFI, there is one instance of the same type of ammunition being the result of your analysis and that's at page 43 of the B/C/S, 38 through 39 of the English in relation to photos 112 and 113 in relation to TOM-04-PRD 213T. Now, in relation to all these 7.62 by 25-millimetre pistol cartridges, would you agree with me that the common alternate name for this cartridge is to call it the Tokarev cartridge?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is by 25, not by 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You are correct. Is the 7.62 by 25-millimetre cartridge more commonly known or referred to as the Tokarev cartridge?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Tokarev.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at 1D5456, this is again from the Internet, Wikipedia. Does this appear to be the same type of cartridge, again, with a different potential manufacturer as the one we've been talking about the Tokarev 7.62 by 25-millimetre cartridge?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, instead of bullet, it should read cartridge.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Cartridge has thus far before used in a different context as opposed to bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If -- strike that. Would you agree with me that since this cartridge started to be produced in 1930 many different fire-arms have been chambered to fire this type of cartridge, I would say at least dozens ranging from the Czech CZ 52, the Nagant revolver, the Sterling MK 17, the PPS-43 and the entire Russian TT family of pistols. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you compare samples of known rounds fired from any other Tokarev chambered guns to compare to your disputed samples to see if they shared any common class characteristics?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general characteristics of rounds fired from the Crvena Zastava M57 pistol have -- are also shared by rounds fired from a TT-33 Tokarev pistol. There are different licences issued to different countries and manufacturers for the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our finding, we state that they may originate from bullets fired from a semi-automatic pistol of Crvena Zastava make, M57, but it was not stated that they originate with any certainty from an M57 pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can take a brief look at D1088 in e-court. It's one of the documents from the Prijedor police that we already looked at earlier today, and I believe it's the one dated in June of 1992 listing the inventory of weapons available to that police entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If it helps, that would be number 32671 of the 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Under the first rubric of weapons, we see the second-to-last entry of some 120, 1.62 [sic] mm TT pistols. Would you agree that this pistol is capable of firing the round the same round and have the same characteristics as the M57? And -- and -- that's the first question.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, not entirely clear now what the first question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it that these rounds can be fired by the weapon you mentioned? That's -- was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Second question in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is about the characteristics, isn't it? Because you started with that. Would you then please phrase that question so that the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me then rephrase the original question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To avoid any misunderstanding, we should first correct the transcript. In page 22, line 24, it should read 7.62-millimetre TT.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think to address both Your Honours' points, I'll just restate the question and hopefully get it right this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the document, sir, we see the second to last entry of 120 items listed as 7.62 mm TT pistol. Would you agree that this type of pistol is capable of firing the same round as the M57 pistol?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that the -- the general characteristics of both the M57 and the TT pistol are identical, such that they cannot be distinguished on a fired round?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TT is a jargon or a slang name for the M57 Crvena Zastava pistol. In this document, it is stated as follows, 7.62 mm TT pistol, but it is unknown what the model is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And leave the various models different marks on the basis of their general characteristics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They share the same general characteristics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Franjic, am I correct that as a result of all of your investigations and analysis, you are not able to positively match any of the single ammunition artefacts you examined from Tomasica as having been conclusively fired by a weapon from the inventory of the VRS army so as to exclude all other possibilities?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our written report and expert opinion, there is no marking, be it on a cartridge, round, or parts of rounds, that we ascertained positively the type, model, and make of fire-arm. We did not say positively this or that round originates from a bullet fired from the M48 army rifle of 7.9-millimetre calibre. Instead, we stated that it may have originated from such and such weapon, if I were to use an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which then also, if I understand you well, does not exclude for the possibility that these rounds were fired by weapons which are available to others than the VRS, be it police, be it civilians, be it whomever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what kind of weapon was at the disposal of the VRS or the police. I do not have a position on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, thank you for your patience and four your answers. That completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, any further questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any further re-examination, there is one matter that I think we can deal with without the witness but it's related to a document that Mr. Ivetic used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if we can deal with it without the witness, then I'll first ask my colleagues whether they have any questions. The Chamber has no further questions for you either, Mr. Franjic. This means that this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way for you to The Hague and for answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties, by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. So during cross-examination of Mr. Franjic, Mr. Ivetic showed him a document, P2894, and that was a message from the Prijedor SJB to the Banja Luka CSB reporting on weapons confiscated and it was dated the 2nd of August, 1992. Now that document refers to a request that we -- that requested that information and we have that request in our evidence collection and we think for context it would be appropriate to show that to Your Honours and to tender it, and I understand from Mr. Ivetic that he agrees. So if we could do that now, please, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got no idea what it is but if you just show it briefly on the screen so that we know what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So if we could see 65 ter 10850, please. And this is a -- it's a memorandum from the Prijedor SJB that essentially contains the content of the request that is responding -- that is responded to in P2894, so we read that the Prijedor SJB on the 1st of August received a dispatch number which is the same number referred to P2894 and that that contained the following. And then if we look at the content of the request, we see a reference to the Banja Luka dispatch number 11 May 1992 and we see the reference to a request for information regarding information on weapons, et cetera, confiscated from individuals since the beginning of the forced disarmament action concluded on 31st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be a D number or a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. The document I used already had a P number so we can even add it to that existing exhibit. It is up to Your Honours basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say that you would even consider to add that to the existing exhibit but that's a bit of a problem, I think, we shouldn't do it because then it's unclear what we saw at the time. But I think give it a P number. And the P number would be, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10850 receives number P7439, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7439 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we ask the usher to escort the next witness into the courtroom, it came to my mind several times during cross-examination that Mr. Ivetic was asking questions which was -- which I would have thought I had read the answer already in the report. Has there been -- and there was no re-examination which apparently means there was nothing to question about the questions that were put to the witness in cross-examination. Has it been endeavoured to find agreement on most of what was said or said again in cross-examination, especially many questions about what the witness could not tell us, was there any disagreement about that, that is what came to my mind many, many times during cross-examination. Mr. Ivetic, have you tried to find agreement on what -- especially what the report does not establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, there's been -- we were always available to discuss with the Prosecution issues of that nature. With the time-period that we had to do the work, try to seek experts of our own, and prepare for the examination, we really didn't have time to sit with the Prosecution in detail to go over these. I would also posit that even if some of these items are in agreement given the high publicity of the reopening and Tomasica and the fact that this evidence was considered to be crucial to the Prosecution case, it is necessary for the public and proceeds to highlight and stress what the actual findings are and to see what they mean actually. So that it's very clear what the value of this evidence presented by the Prosecution actually is for purposes of assessing criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if that's done in cross-examination, one could consider that if the parties even agree on it that it would become even more forceful that that exactly the limited scope of what the witness could tell us. I leave it to that, but I would like to encourage the parties again and again to see whether, instead of spending a lot of time on certain issues which seems not to be very much in dispute in court, rather, to settle those matters and use court time more efficiently. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's Ms. Karahasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. And perhaps meanwhile I'll deal briefly with a matter which is a remaining issue from the testimony of Janko Kecman. On the 11th of May of this year, the witness testified and P7376 was marked for identification pending a revised English translation. That's found at transcript pages 35340 to -42. On the 9th of June, the Prosecution informed the Chamber via an e-mail that a revised translation had been uploaded into e-court under document number ID 0201-1673-ET, and the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the English translation of P7376 with the new translation and admits P7376 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I read the transcript reference, I may have misread. It was -- it's -- well, it's not fully -- it's 35340 to 35342. As always, if there's any further dispute about the accuracy of the new translation, the Defence has an opportunity to address the matter within the next 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that your name is Ms. Karahasanovic? I'd like to invite you to make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by the usher. Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Ms. Karahasanovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Jeremy. You find Mr. Jeremy to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good morning, Ms. Karahasanovic.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'll start by asking you to state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Elmira Karahasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your current professional position?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I am currently assigned to work as the head of section for biological expertise in the federal police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that's the federal police administration of which country?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The federal police administration of my own country, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you recall previously providing a copy of your CV to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31102 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Karahasanovic, on the left side of the screen before you, do you recognise this document as the CV that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And does this provide details about your education, professional training, and professional expertise?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 31102 as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31102 receives number P7440, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. For the Defence since I see no lectern so I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Me again, Your Honours. We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Karahasanovic, did you at the request of the prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina prepare a forensic report dated the 29th of April, 2014 relating to certain artefacts that were found in the Tomasica grave?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31095 on our screens. And just while that's coming up, we also have a clean copy, unmarked copy of the report and the accompanying photo documentation which, with the leave of the Chamber and Mr. Ivetic's consent, I'd ask the kind assistance of the usher to provide to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No problem. And it can go straight to the witness. I do not need to check it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Ms. Karahasanovic, just looking on the screen -- on the left side of the screen, do you recognise this page as the cover page of the report that you -- that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's an accompanying document which was issued by the federal police administration. It was signed by its director, Mr. Dragan Lukac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we have the English now. If we could go do page 2 please in each document, each language. Now, Ms. Karahasanovic, on the screen before us, we see -- we see a letter, it's dated -- or a document dated 29th of April 2014 and we see a reference to subject, and a reference to biological, chemical and dactyloscopic forensic analyses. Now does your expertise relate to all of these particular areas of forensic analysis or just to one particular area?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Only some of them, and those are biological forensic analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And below this heading, we see a reference to an order of the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 17th of March, 2014. Was the analysis in this report carried out pursuant to this particular order?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, could I ask some clarification. You said your expertise is in the field of the biological traces. Now, in the heading of this report, we find three categories. That's biological, chemical and dactyloscopic forensic analyses. I saw in your report that there is some dactyloscopy as well. Do you consider that to be part of the biological aspect, or a separate one? And could you clarify whether you have any specific expertise in the field of dactyloscopy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not authorised to do that. I'm authorised to analyse biological traces. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Karahasanovic, below the reference to the prosecutor's order that we just referred to, we see a list of items and if we can also go to the next page, please, in each language. Now within this list of items, we see a reference to gloves and on the second page here we see towards the bottom we see a reference to two gas masks and also a reference to two fire extinguishers and all of these items referred to were found in the grave during the exhumation. Now, did you personally recover these items from Tomasica mass grave or were they provided to you?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not participate in the location of the material. We received the material from the prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina for further analysis. The analysis of biological, chemical, toxicological and dactyloscopic traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the information about where the items were found, was that information also provided to you by the office of the prosecutor of B and H?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, only what is listed in the order of the prosecutor's office. You have a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So this information that we see here in the report that, for example, a particular glove was found in the grave, was that information about where the glove was found, was that conveyed to you by the BiH office of the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was an integral part of their order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 4 in each document -- each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Ms. Karahasanovic, we see towards the top of the page a reference to what the forensic tests required to establish and we see, for example, the request that DNA traces are to be on the gloves received to be analysed, paying special attention to the analysis of the inner part of the glove. Now, below that, we see a reference to findings and we see the subheading: Biological and DNA forensic analyses. Now, is this particular part of the report analysis that you, yourself, personally conducted?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in this section, we see reference to a number of photographs. Are these photographs contained in the photo booklet that accompanies your report?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we'll look at that shortly. And if we could skip ahead, please, to page 19 in the English and 18 in the B/C/S. And, Ms. Karahasanovic, this is the opinion section of the report. We see the heading: Opinion. And we see the subheading: Biological and DNA forensic report. Does this particular part of the report reflect your own personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we could go do the last page, please, of the report in each language. Now, Ms. Karahasanovic, here we see a reference to forensic analysis by and we see your name and a signature. The two names below that, were those the other two persons who completed the additional analysis contained within this report?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From a colleague, the expert in dactyloscopy and the expert in chemical analysis, on the right-hand side, are the persons who controlled the analysis. The person who was in charge of dactyloscopy is Muamer Kavazovic and Mrs. Iva Trezner was in charge of chemical analysis. At the bottom is signature of the head of the centre who is our chief officer and there is Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Karahasanovic, can you repeat the final name that you mentioned, please.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of centre for the IT of federal police administration of -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Sead Selman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And was there a single person who was responsible for project management for compiling this particular report?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a complex project which required the expertise of experts of different knowledge. I was in charge of the whole project. I organised the entire project. We had to start working together. We had to find the traces which would be processed in various laboratories, depending on their importance and type.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask for the report to be marked for identification at this point pending completion of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31095 receives number P7441, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Karahasanovic, you mentioned that there was an accompanying booklet of photo documentation in respect to this report and I'd like to take a look at that now. Could we please see 65 ter 31096. And as that's coming up, Ms. Karahasanovic, was there a particular person who requested that this booklet of photo documentation be prepared?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted my findings to be accompanied by photos to illustrate the material that was submitted for analysis, the way how it was transported, i.e. how it was packaged, and what traces we used for biological, i.e., DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we now have that document on the screen before us. Do you recognise what you see on the screen before you as the book of photo documentation that you commissioned?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I requested a booklet of photos to be prepared. I could not give any orders. I had to address the chief of centre, and he was the one who initiated the procedure from the moment the material was received, inspected, and selected for analysis, and all that is illustrated by the photos that you can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And let's just take a quick look at one example from this booklet. Could we please go to page 91. I think we can take the English document off the screen, please. Ms. Karahasanovic, just very briefly, can you tell us what we are looking at on this page.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: What we are looking at is some of the material that was submitted for analysis. The marking is 60B and represents parts of a gas mask. Both these photos depict parts of a gas mask.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did -- the details of the analysis of these particular parts of the gas mask are contained in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe that one of the following photos depicts the places from which swabs were taken for further DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I'd ask that the report to be marked for identification pending completion of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31096 receives number P7442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I've no further questions in direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. Ms. Karahasanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find Mr. Ivetic standing to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, madam.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to, first of all, return to P7440 that has been admitted. That is a copy of your curriculum vitae. And while we wait for the English I think I can ask the question I want to ask about your biology degree that you obtained. Did your education or course work for your biology degree include any work in forensic biology?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can turn to page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S, under training courses, it is listed you attended all the courses from the field of forensics and specialist courses from the field of forensic biology. If I could first ask you: How many such courses on forensics did you attend?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: At least 10 or 15 courses. As many as I could afford, i.e., as many as were paid by my institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And these courses that you attended, who were the persons or entities that presented these courses?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Some of the courses took place along time ago, so I can't remember. And as for the others, the most relevant ones took place in the police centre in Zagreb called Ivan Vucetic. One part of the course on using database or CODIS took place in Washington. I don't remember the lectures as well as I do the stuff that I learned at those courses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now I'd like to ask you about the other part of that, the specialist courses in the field of forensic biology. How many of those type of courses did you attend?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Forensic biology. The course lasted six months, if you're only interested in DNA analysis. And there was another course over seven days in Washington, where the topic was using databases. And there was one in Madrid where I spent seven days at the local police centre. We had the opportunity to look at how the material was processed from the moment the traces are selected to the final stage which is electropherogram and the verification or, rather, matching those against their database.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you authored any journal articles on the topics of forensic biology and specifically DNA analysis, forensic DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, within the INGEB seminar which was organised by the Institute for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology in Sarajevo a few years ago. I participated together with my colleagues in the drafting of two papers. I also participated in the publication of an article in forensic literature which is published in my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I note from your CV your membership in the International Association of Criminalists. Was any type of exam or verification process required for such membership?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No. What is required is to pass an exam to become a forensic expert and that is registered in Brcko district. Besides taking that exam, you also need recommendation by your own institution which, in my case, was the federal police administration, as well as the prosecutor's offices of cantonal courts or the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the office of the prosecutor of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Chose to recommendations are mandatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You are a member of the International Association of Identification?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Your Honours, Mr. Jeremy and I are close to a stipulation as to the IAE that was an instruction that you had made last week. And I can tell you that we will have that by the end of this session as Mr. Jeremy has sent me a proposal which I agree with, so we have the information Your Honour requested as to that organisation for Your Honours' review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're looking forward to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think we're at the time for the break. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're at the time of the break. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. And you may now follow the usher and we'd like to see you back at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, did you by any chance forget to tender the expert report of the last witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour, together with the addendum to the expert report. P7434 and P7435 and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I did read your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against the expert report? There are two, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would object based upon matters arising in cross-examination mainly there are no picture comparisons of the matching that was performed so that the expert report does not meet the standards that would be expected for that type of analysis to permit someone to view the same and to comment upon the same from the same -- with the same level of experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is true for both reports, then, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider your objection, and we'll decide in due course. We take a break, and resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom, the two reports by Mr. Franjic are tendered into the evidence. The objections from the Defence are denied. First, no rule exists that everything should be photographed. Second, the material is still in existence, and therefore it's not unfair to admit the report into evidence. Yes, and the numbers are P7434 and P7435. These two reports are admitted into evidence. Mr. Jeremy, the photo documentation, the English version is rather short in e-court. It's two pages. Just saying that there are a lot of photographs. However, the B/C/S version, which is the original, my computer tells me that in e-court the RIV, which has got something with how to produce images, is not capable of showing it to me on my computer. I don't know whether there's any resolution for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So your unable to see the original version on your computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I intend -- it says access violation address so-and-so and error image -- well, at least it gives an error message.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We'll look into that and in terms of the translation I think there are two substantive pages of text in the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I see that but, of course, it doesn't give us access to the images.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Understood. We'll look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, I now to wish to briefly discuss your employment. If we move to page 1 of the CV. I think we can go through this rather quickly. Now in the time-period prior to becoming head of the section for biological expert analyses, that is to say from 1992 onwards, would it be accurate to say that your work at the federal MUP still dealt primarily with biological traces of evidence, and others did the forensic or criminalistic work as to finger-prints?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I have one correction to make. I am not the head of department. I am at a lower rank. I am chief of department for biological analysis. Ever since I began working for the federal police administration I have been working only on biological traces analysis. It excludes finger-printing, analysis or any other sort of analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After you became chief of the department -- biology section of the forensics department of the federal MUP, did you continue to do testing and analysis yourself on investigations in addition to your administrative role as chief?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that is my favourite part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I wish to move to the investigation and analysis of the artefacts recovered from Tomasica. First of all, at the time that your department received the artefacts in question, and now I'm not just referring to the subject matter of the report that Mr. Jeremy went through with you, I'm also talking about the spent cartridges and bullets that your office also analysed. At the time you received these artefacts, did you know that this analysis was potentially going to be used as evidence in the trial against Ratko Mladic here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Franjic testified that the spent bullets and cartridges and that was at transcript page 36400 first went for DNA and finger-print analysis before coming to him and then at transcript page 36401 to 36402, he said that he did know that this was going to be used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should not speak at audible volume at this moment or did till a second ago. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To be fair, I think I'll start from the beginning again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, Mr. Franjic testified at transcript page 36400 and the spent bullet rounds and cartridges received from Tomasica first went for DNA and finger-print analysis before coming to him for his analysis. And then at transcript page 36401 to 36402 he testified that he did know that this investigation and analysis was potentially going to be used in the Mladic proceedings before the Tribunal. How do you account for the fact that Mr. Franjic knew that it was being used for the Mladic case but you did not know it was being used for the Mladic case?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea what Mr. Franjic said. What I do know is what I already said. I didn't know because there wasn't a single sentence in the order we received from the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina that would imply that the material would be used in the trial for which we are here today. The prosecutor's office order was defined in such a way that it referred to unidentified suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In relation to the investigation of these artefacts that you did that are the subject of the report that was tendered today, was there any instruction or deadline to produce quick results from the analysis of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: In the prosecution order, it was defined that the expert analysis needs to be performed within 45 days. I think - and it is my opinion - that we may have used a longer period of time and that that the deadline could have been prolonged, but this is what was defined in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How did that deadline compare as to the deadlines you would normally expect to receive in a case with that many artefacts to be analysed?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was an objective deadline. However, deadlines are not something that cannot be changed, if we put forth a request saying that we need more time to carry out analysis and provide opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were the methods and methodology employed by the forensics department in this case conducted pursuant to any written protocol or procedure?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you in a position or would -- strike that. Would you mind providing a copy of that written protocol to the Court and to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that. When you go back to the federal MUP and when you're in a position to have access to the written protocol, would you mind, at that point in time, providing that document to the Court for use of everyone involved?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, we can do that because there are procedures to be followed when receiving and treating any material for expert analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, as we already mentioned Mr. Franjic, at transcript page 36400, he also indicated that the bags and boxes containing the bullets and cartridges that he reviewed had been processed for DNA and finger-print prior to him receiving them, such that they were received unsealed; the seals had been broken. Do you know who in your department would have unsealed the bags and boxes containing spent bullets and cartridges?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the case, Mr. Bruno Franjic was working in, he was the principal in that case. He was the bearer of the case, and it was done separately from the case we have discussed a moment ago. In other words, nothing was done without his knowledge. It is standard procedure that any rounds and cartridges for ballistic analysis first need to be treated for finger-prints and taking of swabs for DNA analysis after which they are sent for ballistic analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mr. Franjic didn't know who unsealed the materials in question. Does that surprise you, given what you've just said about his role in that other investigation?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic was under an obligation to know who was the person unsealing evidence because he was the principal in the case. I was only responsibility for the case that I acted as principal in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that pursuant to the protocols or procedure in place in the forensic department of the federal MUP there should be a written record kept of the date and identity of persons who take possession of sealed evidence bags and who unseal them?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Such a log must exist in the laboratory or the centre we work at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to shift focus to the containers typically it was bags paper bags, I believe, which were the containers where the gloves, the fire extinguisher, and the gas masks were preserved. Was it you or colleagues of yours on the team that took possession of those items and unsealed the seals existing on those items prior to doing the analysis?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is precisely what is depicted in the photographs attached to the report where I acted as principal. Please define something for me. When you say "the sealing of containers and paper bags," what do you understand by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you when you receive the bags did they have some kind of seal that was dated and signed, sealing the contents in the bags that were used to collect and hold the artefacts.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: That is why I asked you to repeat. The complete forensic material as per procedure needs to be forwarded so that it is sealed and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So we're on the same page. Okay. Great.
