Now ... if we could look very briefly at P7441, MFI, and that is the textual part of the report that you just went through with Mr. Jeremy, and if we can look at page 22 in the English, page 21 in the e-court B/C/S, and you've already identified for us that you were the principal, the person in charge of generating this report and that you were in charge of organising the investigation but that you, yourself, did just the biological analysis. The question I have is in relation to the work of the other two individuals that are listed here. Did you have a role in overseeing, verifying or controlling the work that was done in relation to the finger-print or chemical analysis of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not competent to act in that capacity. At the beginning of my presentation, I said that in the right-hand side corner are the names of people who controlled the work of dactyloscopy analysis and chemical and toxicological analysis. In terms of dactyloscopy, the person in charge it was Muamer Kavazovic. As for the chemical analysis, it was Ms. Eva Trezner.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Iva Trezner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, being the person in charge, or principal, did you have the ability to select the members of the team that would be doing this analysis or did somebody else make that selection for this particular investigation?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The people from the department were involved in it, in other words, myself and my colleague, both experts certified for DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may have missed the gist of the question which was whether it was you who said which experts should do the dactyloscopy and chemical part or whether it was someone else who said it should be Mr. A or Ms. B to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have the right to appoint any experts. The head of department assigns the case to the respective units and the heads of units choose the experts who will take part in the expert analysis work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in relation to the Hatidza Muratovic, we see that they're listed as a monodactyloscopy specialist which, according to my understanding, it relates to the analysis of single finger-prints. Do you know if this individual acquired their specialist skill during law school during their studies, or do they have any other relevant degree that is not listed here?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I'm competent to provide an answer to that question because I am not senior to Ms. Hatidza Muratovic or to any other expert working for another department. Our head is in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked about any knowledge you may have. It has got nothing do with whether you are senior or not. You may know, you may not know. If you know, please tell us; if you don't, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, all of my colleagues are sufficiently expert to work on the parts of analysis entrusted to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was - and then especially in relation to Hatidza Muratovic - whether she acquires her specialist skill when being educated at law school, if you know that, whether she already developed her skills then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't think that she did or you don't think that you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While studying, I don't think she could have acquired any knowledge in terms of forensic analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question, please, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One more question as to Ms. Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long this colleague has been performing finger-print analysis within the same department of the MUP as you?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Between 15 and 18 years, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Jeremy, is the Prosecution going to rely on that part of the expert report for which the responsible expert is not called as an expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's precedence in this case that we have reports tendered into evidence where the underlying experts are not always present within the courtroom so, for example, Dean Manning's provided a report that referred to the expert analysis of experts we didn't, in fact, call. That's P1735. So we feel that these parts of the report should be included in the overall report that is tendered but it's essentially a question of weight that the Chamber will eventually decide to attribute to that part of the report given that the expert themselves, specific experts, not being called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say that it's your view that it's a matter of weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do understand the Prosecution's position. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the results of Ms. Muratovic's work, how did you -- did you receive them and incorporate them into the final report or did she assist in drafting the final report? How did this document that we have now in evidence originate, drawing together the conclusions of three different experts?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Each of these experts wrote their own separate reports. My role was to unify or collate their parts and mine into a joint report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do the original separate reports drafted by each of the other two experts still exist somewhere within the federal MUP in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you be in a position - again, when you go back to Sarajevo - to obtain the same and to produce them to the Court for review by the parties?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to look at page 13 in the B/C/S and it also happens to be page 13 in the English, and I want to focus on the part that begins DNA analysis, which I believe you and I will agree is the part that you know the most about, because you did the work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you perform all of the work alone as to the DNA analysis or did someone else assist you in any aspect of the work?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The rules of my department state that we all take part and there are very few of us there, there are only an additional three experts to me. We all take part in the individual stages of DNA analysis. In other words, we are all included.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say "we are all included," is one of those persons the person who signed as controlling the work on the last page of the report that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say "controlling the work," could you be a little more specific about what that means? How do they exercise that oversight while the work is being performed?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: We are all privy to each stage of the work in terms of applying the procedures and protocols required of certain stages. The results are checked, and at the end of the process, all of the material is put together and discussed jointly. Let me just add that when reviewing the material, we were all included, all of us from the department, meaning myself, the three experts, and our colleague, a lady technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to now look with you at 1D5860. While we wait for the same I can introduce it as being an article from "Forensic On the Scene" an in-the-lab magazine from April 12, 2013 entitled: Touch DNA: From the crime scene to the crime laboratory. And, first of all, I want to ask you if you're familiar with this journal?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 4, I'd like to focus on the bullet points which I will read to you and then ask some questions about. And the bullet points are introduced as follows it says: "In addition to lab coats and masks, how is contamination detected, controlled and monitored? Some examples which may be employed are," and the first bullet point is: "Access to the laboratory shall be controlled and limited to prevent access by unauthorised personnel?" Let me do it this way. In relation to this first bullet point, did your department follow this example to limit contamination of the biological material being examined?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The number one rule in my job is to make sure to prevent any contamination, either from a person to an object or vice versa or among the traces themselves. So it doesn't matter what kind of contamination we're talking about. To that purpose we use protective clothing and all the other things that we need to apply when we start working with the forensic material.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand and I thank you for that answer, but this says "in addition to lab coats and masks, access to the laboratory shall be controlled and limited." Was that done by your department for the investigation that resulted in the report that we have now seen?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: We opened the case together. Or, rather, we opened the artefacts together, not only us from the department but also all the experts that would be involved in the case. The first thing that was needed was to identify all the traces that were to be used in dactyloscopic expertise and then we identified those biological traces that would be processed. In that, our colleague from the Department for Chemical Analysis identified the material that he needed to process, and he did it after we identified our material. The first part of the work was team-work. All the experts were involved if they were requested to participate. We made sure that all the contamination was prevented as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's try that again. In relation to the taking and analysis of DNA samples from the artefacts was the laboratory where that work was performed controlled such that only yourself and the three other -- two other individuals qualified for that work were in the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The department for biological expertise and especially the DNA expertise department is completely separate from the rest of the scan of forensic and IT support department in every stage of such work material is isolated prepared and when it comes to bench-mark samples, those samples are examined in a completely different and separate area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you still missed part of the question. The question very much focussed - if I understood it well, Mr. Ivetic - on whether the access to that laboratory was restricted so that no outsiders could come in. Were there any such measures taken so as to avoid that someone would have access that shouldn't be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I said in the first part of my answer. This department is completely isolated from other departments. The entrance to the department is protected by a coded gate and only the employees have codes that allow them to enter the premises of the department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've talked about separation; I think that handles the next two points. You mentioned bench-mark samples. Now this document talks about "negative controls are being used from evidence examination through extraction and amplification." Is that the same thing as a bench-mark sample; and, if not, could you please explain for us what you meant by bench-mark sample?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The complete material and the traces that were processed for the purpose of this case were disputable traces, i.e., traces about which we did not have any knowledge and we were supposed to establish a DNA profile based on them. Bench-mark samples are those whose origins are known. We know who the individuals were who provided those bench-mark samples, and the only thing that needs to be established in such cases is to establish a DNA profile.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And these bench-mark samples, is one of the bench-mark samples that would be normally obtained required for every staff member or analyst dealing with DNA so as to create an elimination profile for any DNA that is discovered in evidence that might have been the result of inadvertent contamination?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Those samples are control samples. Not only in this case but in any other case dealt with by our department. There are DNA profiles that need to be checked to avoid contamination. And what I meant when I used the term "bench-mark samples" are samples taken from known individuals. They were submitted for possible comparison with the DNA profiles of -- of disputable traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's what confused me. For purposes of the analysis you did here there were no bench-mark sample, were there?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could return to P7441 MFI, and page 19 in the English and page 18 in the B/C/S, this will again be in the section containing the DNA findings. And in this section and the pages that follow, you reach four unique DNA profiles, one female and three male, all of them NN or unknown. Am I correct in concluding that these DNA profiles would most likely belong to those individuals that wore the gloves, given where these samples were obtained?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you talk about DNA profiles whereas the report repeatedly says partial DNA profile, which is not the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the first one does not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Incomplete" is still not a DNA profile.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed. Agreed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Irrespective of the completeness of a DNA profile, a DNA profile is a DNA profile. This is just my remark. And when it comes to your question, whether this concerns the DNA of the person who wore gloves, I can't be sure of that. I can't say that it can does concern that person. The samples for obtaining those DNA profiles were taken from the inside of the glove. So the DNA profile in this case was obtained from the inside of the glove and not from the person who either wore or didn't wear those gloves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion again. Mr. Ivetic asks you whether he is correct when he concludes that if a DNA profile is taken from the inside of a glove, whether it's most likely that the DNA profile would match, although you don't have any comparison, would match with the person - still unknown - who had worn that glove.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For a moment, I'd like to return to the spent bullets and cartridges that were the subject of the report that Mr. Franjic was the principal of and he in his report stated that after they were received -- after they went through the DNA and finger-print analysis, he then cleaned them with a solution of water, 10 per cent vinegar, and acetone. Would you agree that this treatment of those artefacts by this solution would at that stage destroy any remaining DNA and/or finger-print trace material?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the final stage of analysis. This is ballistic analysis. And after that stage, it is no longer possible to look for either prints or DNA molecules or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, prior to being cleaned by this solution the bullets and cartridges would be I presume covered in dirt, mud, other material, how does your department obtain -- or ascertain whether there is useful DNA or finger-print material on those artefacts if they are covered in, let's say, mud?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to finger-prints, I wouldn't answer because this falls within the scope of other people's expertise. When it comes to DNA analysis, swabs were taken after dactyloscopic examination from the surface of the artefacts and they were treated in our further work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But would you agree that that method would not gain access to any trace DNA or finger-print material under the mud? You only swab the visible portions of the item, not that which is covered in mud or some other substance.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Swabs were taken from the surface, which means that it doesn't really matter whether the surface was muddy and dirty or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess I'm trying to find out does your department -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If it assists and, you know, looking at Mr. Franjic's report, I'm happy to agree with Mr. Ivetic that it clearly states that there was no DNA or insufficient amount of human DNA molecules for further individualisation in respect to the cartridges analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Except for that which was potentially lost by the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that's clear. I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A saying comes to my mind, Mr. Ivetic, that you can't eat your cake and have it. If you want to clean certain objects and if that would perhaps remove traces, if you would not -- if you would not clean it, you would not go below that dirt and -- but apart from that, you would have expected more -- better results from any underlying material because, as we see now, if we're talking about DNA testing, and this witness does not testify about finger-printing, then it's mainly that almost nothing was found and that it was not material, DNA material, which could be compared, that the only thing I think that was really established, that the DNA samples apart from one being from a female and three from men, that it would not be the same men. Not much more is established in this report, if I understand it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we're mixing reports. The issue of the cleaning only relates to the cartridges not to the four unique profiles. Those relate to the gloves which is a separate issue. And although [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... nothing was found on the cartridges --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if I understand the report well could be prejudicial for your client. If nothing is found, there's not much to be established contrary to the interests of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence would say for purposes of all three reports nothing is prejudicial to our client is found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, that's, of course, the reason why I earlier indicated that I was slightly surprised that there was no agreement on -- especially on what was not established because not much has been established. And if we would focus on that, that might be an efficient use of our time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to look at page 15 in the English and 15 in the B/C/S, and this is the part of the report that you were the principal of, done by colleague, the finger-printing specialist. From -- first of all, from your work in being the principal and organising the investigation and the drafting of this report, did you reference or consult any reference materials or publications relating to the process of seeking finger-print trace evidence from the interior of gloves before signing this report?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: For the umpteenth time, I'm going to say that I am not a finger-printing expert. When it comes to check whether there were papillary line traces or not. I didn't participant in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we're coming close to the time where we have to take a break --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'd like to raise a brief matter in one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'd like to see you back after 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hvala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a quick scheduling inquiry for Mr. Ivetic and perhaps for the Bench in connection with the next witness. So it's principally a matter of how much time may remain with the cross and whether or not we can excuse the next witness for the remainder of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be close. I'm thinking approximately half an hour remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wouldn't make it useless to keep the next witness on stand by. What I wanted to raise in ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it depends on how much you would have in re-examination. If you say I need another ten or 15 minutes in re-examination then, of course, the next witness could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, at this point, I have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Jeremy, when I earlier asked you whether the Prosecution would rely on a part of a report which was not -- where the author of that part of the report would not be called as an expert, you referred to practice in this case, especially you referred to Mr. Manning. Now if I read page 14156 of the transcript, if I read the following and the question starts the previous page: "Do those reports also contain separate, in fact, relating to your separate individual involvement in the exhumation project? "Yes, they do, Your Honours. I examined the reports and the underlying data, the autopsy reports and the photographs which had formed the basis of the reports made by the experts but because, for instance, the chief archaeologist may have only been in the field for one season, he would not have seen in depth the previous materials or the material that came after him so I was examining all the material across the board." And then it's how it continues. That's pretty different from the situation we find with this witness, and I just wanted to ask you again whether it is on the basis of that one example which you mentioned and of which I read only a very small portion which gives a totally different picture as far as the involvement of Mr. Manning in the reports of others is concerned. Whether you still take the position that the practice by this Chamber in relation to Mr. Manning would justify that we would rely on the dactyloscopical part of report and the chemical part of the report where this witness repeatedly said that she can't give any answer about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I take the point that the situations are different to an extent. The witness has told us that she had an overview supervisory role in pulling the report together. I accept that she's been very clear about the limits of her expertise. Although I think the position of the Prosecution is that those parts of the report should still be included because they relate to the thoroughness and the integrity of the investigation conducted by the witness and her colleagues, although, again, I accept that -- or it's the position of the Prosecution that it will be a question of weight to which the Chamber chooses to put on those parts of the report when we don't call the underlying experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the position. We take a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the same point, Mr. Jeremy, while she did tell us that she was -- took -- she -- she participated in a supervisory position the detail of that supervision related to her collating the reports without being able to comment on any of the parts that she didn't author. So, really, it was not supervisory; it was just collating.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that Your Honour, that it was a supervisory role in terms of collating different aspects of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom, Mr. Jeremy, the Chamber decided that it will not rely on the dactyloscopy part or the chemical part of the report co-authored by this witness, unless the other authors would be called as experts. They were not on your list, and if I say the Chamber will not rely on it, it still would be a question what there is at all to rely on. That's rather limited. And that's true, both for Prosecution and Defence, as far as we can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you'll keep this in mind when continuing your cross-examination, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours and I will eliminate some questions, but I think some questions still are necessary to determine the methodology use, and the intent behind the investigation to the extent it may taint the results of other parts of the investigation, whether proper methodology was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine that you want to explore the intent of the investigation, whether the methodology -- unless you have good reasons to believe that the methodology was adapted for any purpose to that, but then please put that in clear questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Madam, in response to my prior question before the break you said that you are not authorised, my simple question was did you look at any reference materials regarding the process of seeking finger-prints from the interior of gloves as part of this investigation? Either you did or you didn't. Surely you know whether you did or didn't irrespective of your expertise.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, could we get the answer again. Is it I did or I did not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I did review part of material whereby it was sought to confirm whether any finger-prints were present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me just make sure that we're not misunderstanding. Are -- when I use the words "reference material" I mean books, journals and other work done by others talking about the process, not the actual investigation that you -- that your -- that your lab did. Is your answer yes, I did, does it relate to outside material that others drafted about the field or about -- or it does it relate to material that your colleagues in a laboratory provided?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: My answer had to do with the following. I reviewed the part of the report that had to do with the identification of the presence of finger-prints on the material forwarded to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was whether you consulted any articles, books, instructions, whatever standards of -- did you -- for the finger-printing, did you consult any of such materials?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now we're clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in the photographs that we have on the screen it would appear that the tips of the fingertips of the latex or plastic rubber gloves have been cut open by scissors. In other cases you worked on within the federal MUP is it the normal procedure for the forensic department to cut open the fingers of gloves to seek the presence of and to analyse finger-print trace evidence as was done in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it is a fact that these are cut or just what you suspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that the description says that they were cut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that so? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Incisions were made on the gloves, in the area of fingers and on the sides. That's what the report says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... but your question is premised on the belief that they were cut. So can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, incision is something else, yeah. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you in a position to answer my question? As to the work done by your department in prior cases, are always incisions made to cut open the fingers of gloves to analysis them for finger-print trace evidence?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can only discuss this case where I worked as a member of the team. That is to say, together with other experts. In this case, no cuts or incisions were made to the finger part of the glove. It was the entire glove that was cut on the side in order for us to be able to examine the inside of the glove. In the order from the prosecutor's office from Bosnia-Herzegovina it was stated that particular attention should be paid to the inside of the gloves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, madam, the literature I've looked at for this type of review, in those instances, the gloves are left intact when reviewing. Would you be surprised to learn that?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The only way to access the tips of fingers is to cut the glove across the side. It was the decision of the experts engaged in finger-print analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So they made the decision. That's fine. We'll leave that for them then. Now if we turn to ... if we turn to the next page in English and in B/C/S, we see at the end of the day that only two of the glove artefacts were reviewed and they were subjected to a method of cyanoacrylate in a fuming chamber. As a biologist would you agree that exposing the artefacts to cyanoacrylates would destroy any remaining biological or DNA evidence that might exist on those artefacts?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I would agree with you, but it was preceded by taking samples for DNA analysis. In other words, after the gloves were treated for finger-printing, no further biological traces analysis was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does that not then prevent another expert from double-checking that work if no further DNA samples could be taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you be very precise on what work you mean. Do you mean the taking of a sample or do you mean to repeat the DNA analysis of the sample taken by the swabs? Which of the two do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To take a DNA sample from the artefacts and to analyse that DNA sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness was implicitly answered that question by saying that it would destroy any remaining DNA traces. Is that well understood, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And my follow-up question would be: Would the swab still be available to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... repeat DNA testing from that sample already taken before the object was treated in the way you described it for finger-print --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No swab can be taken after such treatment of a glove in the respect of that kind of dactyloscopic analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the originally taken samples, they are still existing? Could you -- you are nodding, but could you speak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. They are preserved as isolates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to move to the gas masks that we talked about. If we can look at P7441, MFI, page 17 in both languages, and it's going to be paragraph 1. Paragraph 1 at the bottom in the English and in the B/C/S. And in describing the mask it says here: "Drab olive rubber masks such as those used by the JNA as military equipment." Now, and we saw the photograph earlier in direct examination. Now, one of the tasks for the analysis recorded at page 4 of this report was to determine the model and manufacture of the mask. What steps or research were undertaken to fulfil this task of determining the model and manufacturer of the mask.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The page you are referring to and the paragraph in question makes part of the expert analysis conducted by the department for chemical and toxicological analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So is the answer you do not know what steps were taken to determine the model and manufacturer of the mask?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was only able to read it, like you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to your proofing note rather quickly, 1D5867, in paragraph 4, it says that you told the Prosecution: "Asked about the reference to the JNA in para 1 on page 17 of the English version of the expert report ... the witness indicated that this part of the report was prepared by a colleague (referenced in the report), but believed this JNA reference was intended to function as an example of who might have used the drab olive rubber mask referred to in this paragraph?"

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are you now telling us that the chemical analyst is the one who inserted this reference to a military equipment mask usually worn by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: As an expert, I wouldn't interpret this sentence in that sense. The sentence in question is as follows: Such as ones used as the military equipment of the JNA. So it provides for the possibility that they might have been used as part of -- or part of JNA equipment. It is not an assertion. It is a possibility. At least that's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, to the extent you'd like to make the point that it was not compared with the Panamanian army or the Korean army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no that's not the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that it was focussed, therefore, especially on this army for an example, then that point would be clear. If you have another point to make, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As the principal in charge of this report and having in page 4 of that report an instruction to determine the make and manufacturer of the masks in question, would you have expected your colleague to check and confirm if, in fact, there's only one manufacturer of such masks in the former Yugoslavia and whether they produced the same masks for both army and civilian use, according to the literature from 1960 through 1995.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as you sit here, you do not know whether he did that research and confirmed those facts that I've just presented to you?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could just briefly look at 1D5855, and if we could go to page 2, this is a reference material on Yugoslavian-make equipment and we have here two very similar looking olive-drab masks. One the M1, the other, the MC1. One military, one civilian. Did your colleague ever mention to you in the -- in the process of preparing his report that there existed a civilian model of a mask that resembled a military model of a mask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness has been clear in that she doesn't know what research was conducted by her colleague in respect to this mask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether in preparing the report your colleague said something about a civilian version of such a gas mask. Did he say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the point being that the focus has been on military equipment in this area and that other alternatives are not sufficiently explored. If that's your point you'd like to make - and I earlier presented in a rather limited way, foreign and local, now it's army, non-army - that point is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your report, the last part that I want to discuss with you is the extinguisher which is identified as being a Pastor make, and if we can have the photographic documentation which I believe is P7442, at page 105 of the B/C/S. Now, it's hard to see from the photographs in the documentation, are -- are these what would be referred as 6-kilogram capacity extinguishers manufactured by Pastor in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: What I can answer is as follows. The two gas extinguishers were forwarded for forensic analysis as marked in the prosecution order, they were produced by Pastor and their respective numbers were one and two. I only relied on such data to ascertain the existence of any biological traces on the items. As you can read from my part of the report, any other designation or detail was something that was performed by the same colleague who wrote the part of the report that had to do with the masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But in performing your review you actually had the physical extinguisher in your possession. Is it a 6-kilogram or is it a larger container?

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I really didn't weigh them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could just briefly look at 1D5858, this is an ad --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber will not rely on 6-kilogram, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I earlier indicated that, most important is that the witness identified that the photographed extinguishers as the one she examined on the presence of biological traces and that's what seems to be most relevant at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Madam, this, is an advertisement for an automobile equipment company that lists a 6-kilogram Pastor extinguisher as being equipment for a -- for trucks. Did your colleague doing the analysis of the extinguisher at any point in time make any determination that this type of extinguisher was used for any type of specific vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you know, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you know, yeah.

utterances.speaker: ELMIRA KARAHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Madam, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm glad to say I'm done and I'm at the 30-minute mark so hopefully we can finish with the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Jeremy, any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Only to tender the report and the photo documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we don't need the witness for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karahasanovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for answering all the questions that you were put to you, by the parties, put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again, and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, the numbers that were assigned were?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: P7441 to the report, and P7442 to the accompanying photo documentation, both MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, apart from not relying upon the material that was done by the other experts, the position of the Defence is that, given that we are unable to challenge and cross-examine those experts to determine why their portions of the report were written in the way that they were, we are unable to get to the truth of the matter of the methodology that was employed, why it was employed, and what the intent behind the investigation was. Which would have a bearing on the weight that Your Honours would place upon any evidence arising from the investigation. So we believe that in order for these reports to be tendered, irrespective of whether you're going to rely upon the findings of the experts, those other two experts should be made available to the Defence to cross-examine on the record and to thus provide that missing detail as to why portions of the report were undertaken in the manner that they were undertaken which these -- which this witness of the Prosecution chose to present was unable to address. Thank you. And, further, I note that I forgot to tendered 1D5855 which I would tender at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first deal with that. Any objection, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 1D5855 would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D1090, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Any response, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just simply to say, Your Honours, that I think Your Honours are in a position to assess the methodology employed by the witness in respect to parts of the report in which she authored. I'm not sure I quite understand Mr. Ivetic's reference to the intent of the investigation, although I would note that the order from the prosecutor requesting this analysis be conducted has been provided to the Defence, and Mr. Ivetic has chosen not use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your objection to admission is denied, which means that P7441 and P7442 are admitted into evidence. And I refer to what is already on the record, that the Chamber will not rely on the -- any findings related to the dactyloscopy and the chemical examination of the materials. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours. Mr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Clark be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution is ready to call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would be Mr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Clark. The -- you testified before in this case. You've made a solemn declaration that you'd speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind that you that solemn declaration is still binding upon you when now giving further evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, you will only be with us for a very short time and for a longer time tomorrow. You'll first be examined by Ms. D'Ascoli, and not as a surprise for you, she is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Although your name has been mentioned already, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: John Clark.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I'm a forensic pathologist. I'm in a semi-retired state at the moment but I'm still a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you testified as an expert before this Tribunal in a number of cases.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Including this case before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you recall providing a copy of your curriculum vitae to the Office of the Prosecutor when testifying as an expert in this case in September 2013?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If can I please have -- call up P2256.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, once the document -- here it is. Sir, do you recognise the document now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Is this a copy of your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: It's a copy of the curriculum vitae at that time, yes. Obviously there have been a number of minor changes since then, but nothing -- nothing substantial.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you please tell us any update to this CV.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: It says at the beginning my current position was as a full-time research student now. That is rather on hold at the moment because of other commitment and other work I have been asked to do which is included work for the International Criminal Court in work in Africa. So that has rather put things on hold. But that's really the main -- there's various other minor roles which have slightly changed but it's substantially the same CV.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. And by now, you have been a forensic pathologist for about 30 years; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. 30 or more years, probably 33 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, before we continue I note that you have a folder in front of you. Can you please tell the Court what you have in there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I have three documents. One is the report which I produced for the courts on the Tomasica cases. The second one is a table, a lengthy table, with lots of details of the individual cases which was the basis of the -- the report. And thirdly is a short summary document which summarizes the findings in the main table.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would ask that Dr. Clark is allowed to use -- to refer to this document and the Defence can, of course, inspect this documents. We didn't have time to do it beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first ask the witness whether, especially the summary, whether you'd -- would give it for inspection to the Defence if they would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assumed that they had already seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If it's a summary already disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it is one of the three documents that will be tendered as part of Dr. Clark's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If is all disclosed material and if it will be tendered into evidence, then the only thing the Chamber would ask you is to make clear when you are consulting those documents and when you're giving your testimony from pure recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, did you at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal prepare a report dated the 21st of April, 2014 on the autopsy findings from the human remains recovered from the Tomasica mass grave in 2013?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please bring up 65 ter 31090.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, while this is coming up, can you describe the nature of your role or assistance in the post-mortem examinations of the bodies recovered from the Tomasica grave-site.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Recalled]
utterances.text: My role was a little different from my previous roles in connection with this court. Previously I was in an official role as the chief pathologist. This was an informal role, this time, for Tomasica. I was particularly interested in this area really from more a research point of view, and I approached the pathologists, the local Bosnian pathologist to see if I would be able to learn of the findings at some stage. But more than that, they invited me to actually take part in the work. They very much welcomed that and my past experience. The ICMP, International Commission on Missing Persons, as did ICTY. So I took part in the post-mortem examinations, a very active part, physically engaged in the post-mortems, along with the two local pathologists, Dzevad Durmisevic and Nermin Sarajlic. And it was all a very co-operative exercise; we shared findings, showed each other things. I took my own notes and photographs, they took their own similar notes and photographs. They will have produced individual autopsy reports for each case as was their official role. I did not do that but instead produced the table, the big -- the thick document which I have submitted, which really is a -- a kind of general summary of all the autopsy findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. Maybe it a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is a good time. Although very quickly, Mr. Clark, that we have to adjourn already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, the 1st of July - yes, I always have to think about whether the month has 30 or 31 days - the 1st of July, 9.30 in the morning. But you're excused only after I have instructed that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way, with whomever it may be, about your testimony, whether the little bit of testimony given today or still testimony to be begin tomorrow, but it also includes previous testimony given in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I fully understand that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn, and we resume 1st of July, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
